title.rendered: How was Ekiti gov poll? A good question!

content.rendered:
THIS is a very good question to begin with: How did the 2026 Ekiti State governorship poll fare in terms of credibility, transparency, deployment of logistics by the umpire, voter turnout, and the release of results? This is pertinent because, since pre-independence, Nigeria’s elections have remained fractious, violent, and contentious.

Things have degenerated in the Fourth Republic, where the courts have supplanted the will of the electorate by regularly deciding election winners.

So, the off-season ballot in Ekiti, which produced Biodun Oyebanji of the All Progressives Congress as the winner, was held under this dark cloud on June 20.

A total of 13 political parties participated in the election. The incumbent, Oyebanji, polled 319,224 votes and swept the majority of votes in all 16 local government areas. Oyebanji defeated his closest co-contestants, Wole Oluyede of the Peoples Democratic Party, who scored 40,533 votes, and Dare Bejide of the African Democratic Congress, who got 12,872 votes.

The poll is the first time a governor has won consecutive terms since 1999.

INEC gave a good account of itself in the area of logistics and processing of results. According to media reports, voting materials arrived early, and most polling centres were opened for operations by 8.30 am.

The results from 2,379 of the 2,445 polling units had been uploaded by 4 pm on Election Day. As confirmation, INEC recorded on its platform that the percentage uploaded in the election was 97.75.

After 27 years of democracy, the election was still an admixture of highs and lows, hopes and deep anxieties.

There were pockets of crises in a few LGAs, but the election was largely peaceful in line with the previous off-cycle elections since 2014.

The 2026 governorship election was also adjudged credible.

However, it was characterised by low voter turnout and vote buying.

There were discrepancies in the number of political parties that participated in the election and the number of registered voters.

It was also alleged that 1,059,360 voters were registered, but 988,251 were recorded in the results sheets. This confused the media, which quoted different figures in their reports.

Voter turnout was pegged at 37 per cent, nominally up from the 36.47 per cent recorded in the 2022 polls. This is a far cry from the 49.12 per cent recorded in the 2014 first off-cycle election – the highest turnout since 1999.

Ekiti’s 37 per cent voter turnout reinforces the declining trend of off-cycle governorship elections from 2022 and their possible implications for the 2027 general elections.

With 37 per cent voter turnout, the election recorded the second-lowest in the state’s electoral history. In the other off-cycle elections, Ekiti recorded 50.32 per cent in 2014; 44.36 per cent in 2018; and 36.5 per cent in 2022.

The off-cycle election in Osun recorded a voter aggregate of 42.37 per cent in 2022. Kogi, Imo, and Bayelsa states had 43.32 per cent, 29.41 per cent, and 27.55 per cent, respectively, in 2023. In 2024, Ondo recorded 24.79 per cent, while Edo had 26.59 per cent, with Anambra on 21.34 per cent in 2025.

Local council and by-elections were no exceptions.

Therefore, more needs to be done to improve the voter turnout in the Osun off-cycle governorship election in August.

But the Ekiti exercise was marred by vote-buying. Reports stated that cash inducements ranging from N5,000 to N15,000 were shared at the polling units.

Media reports indicated that, rather than distributing cash at some of the polling units, party agents issued “numbered slips after voting.” Name-writing after voting was employed to induce voters and outwit anti-corruption agencies.

Ekiti State joined the off-season governorship election family after the declaration of Olusegun Oni of the Peoples Democratic Party as the winner of the 2007 governorship election was overturned by the judiciary. In turn, Kayode Fayemi of the defunct Alliance for Democracy was declared the authentic winner by the Court of Appeal in 2010.

The discrepancies observed in the Ekiti election are developments that INEC has to address. They are a bad omen for the 2027 general elections. 

So, there must be massive, coordinated, and urgent moves to sensitise people in local languages to the need to shun financial inducement from politicians who are out to compromise their rights and mortgage the destinies of future generations.

Again, the voters must take their destinies into their own hands and prioritise their rights over pots of soup.

The arrested offenders must be prosecuted.

All this makes Nigerians ask: Will INEC be able to address these concerns ahead of the Osun governorship election and the 2027 general elections?
